item.title: Peru's move to reconsider protections for Mashco Piro raises fears of Amazon logging
item.description:
Peru's move to reconsider protections for Mashco Piro raises fears of Amazon logging
Indigenous leaders in Peru are warning that a government decision to reconsider protections for the Mashco Piro could expose their Amazon rainforest territory to loggingBySTEVEN GRATTAN Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 6:24 PM
MEXICO CITY -- Indigenous leaders in Peru are warning that a government decision to reconsider protections for one of the world’s largest uncontacted Indigenous groups could expose more of their Amazon rainforest territory to logging, raising fears of violent encounters and the spread of life-threatening diseases.
The Mashco Piro, who live deep in the forests of southeastern Peru and avoid contact with outsiders to preserve their traditional way of life, have increasingly been spotted near encroaching logging concessions in recent years, highlighting growing pressure on their ancestral lands.
Eusebio Rios Iviche, vice president of the Indigenous organization FENAMAD, told The Associated Press on Monday the decision threatens to reverse years of efforts to protect the Mashco Piro, exposing them to greater risks of encounters with outsiders and diseases to which they have little immunity.
The controversy centers on a 2016 government study that recommended expanding the Madre de Dios Territorial Reserve, a protected area established in 2002 for the Mashco Piro and other Indigenous peoples living in isolation.
A government commission responsible for protecting isolated Indigenous peoples decided last week to revisit that study rather than proceed with the proposed expansion, according to Indigenous organizations and the advocacy group Survival International.
The move has raised concerns that logging concessions overlapping with the proposed expansion could continue operating in areas Indigenous organizations say are essential to the Mashco Piro’s survival.

item.title: Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard searches for at least 5 missing after boat crash
item.description:
Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard searches for at least 5 missing after boat crash
Authorities in Trinidad and Tobago are conducting search and rescue operations for several people missing after a boating accidentByThe Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 6:08 PM
Share
PORT-OF-SPAIN, Trinidad -- Authorities in Trinidad and Tobago said search and rescue operations were being conducted on Monday for several people who went missing after a boating accident.
Crews spent most of Monday searching for at least five people who were reported missing after the collision, according to the Hunters Search and Rescue Team, a local nongovernmental organization that assisted authorities with the search.
The Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard said two boats collided on Sunday evening in waters off the northwestern peninsula of Trinidad, the larger of the two main islands that make up the twin-island Caribbean nation.
“Preliminary reports indicate that several persons remain unaccounted for as search efforts continue,” the coast guard said in a statement on Monday.
As the two vessels collided, one vessel pitched into the air, throwing its occupants into the water, according to eyewitness Jonathan Salandy, a boat captain with local tour company Pontoon Tours TT.
“I saw people just in the water all over,” Salandy said in a video statement.
Salandy said he and his crew raced toward the scene and began rescuing survivors under the cover of darkness. He said they threw life jackets out to the crash victims and pulled some of the victims on to the tour boat.

item.title: Pope meets with survivors of clergy abuse in Argentina as it reckons with legacy and ongoing cases
item.description:
Pope meets with survivors of clergy abuse in Argentina as it reckons with legacy and ongoing cases
Pope Leo XIV have met with survivors of clergy abuse during his visit to ArgentinaByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press and ALMUDENA CALATRAVA Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 3:34 PM
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV met with survivors of clergy abuse on Monday during his visit to Argentina, a country that has been reckoning with the Catholic Church’s legacy of sex abuse and cover-up, including in cases in which the Argentine Pope Francis intervened.
The Vatican said Leo spent about an hour meeting individually, and then as a group, with five victims of abuse by clergy and “church institutions” who were chosen by the local church. The meeting took place at the Catholic University of Argentina.
Leo listened to their “painful stories and proposals to consolidate paths of healing in the church,” said a statement from Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni.
Acknowledging that there were other groups of victims who had wanted to meet with Leo, “the pope expressed his closeness and desire to reinforce paths of protection, of welcome and accompaniment in the church,” it said.
Victims groups had said they wanted to meet with Leo and were denied, including a group of 43 women who allege they were subjected to human trafficking and forced labor at centers of the conservative group Opus Dei in Argentina.
Their allegations implicate senior members of Opus, some of whom have been formally accused in a criminal investigation into the women's claims. Prosecutors have requested that the members be summoned for questioning, but the judge has not ordered it. Opus has denied wrongdoing.

item.title: Honduran court delays verdict in disappearance case that exposed sex trafficking ring
item.description:
Honduran court delays verdict in disappearance case that exposed sex trafficking ring
A Honduran court has postponed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie PeñaByANNA-CATHERINE BRIGIDA Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 2:28 PM
Share
MEXICO CITY -- A Honduran court postponed a verdict Monday in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Peña, delaying a decision until Nov. 20 as relatives, lawyers and women's rights groups demanded justice.
The case has drawn attention to allegations of impunity and corruption that advocates say have allowed widespread gender violence in the Central American country.
Four men are on trial for crimes related to Peña’s disappearance. Two U.S. citizens, Harold Green and William James Murdock, face human trafficking charges, while another U.S. citizen, Gary Lee Johnston, and Honduran Gustavo Trejo are accused of criminal association.
The case has implicated public officials and exposed a criminal ring known as “Delta Teams” that has drawn comparison to the Jeffrey Epstein network in a country with high rates of gender violence and low conviction rates for related crimes.
Lawyers representing the family have questioned the lack of transparency of the investigation and trial, which was not open to the press or general public. Peña's family said it has received death threats, and the August killing of Dereck McNeil, a key protected witness, further exposed the dangers of seeking justice in Honduras.
“There are many more women and girls who have been victims of trafficking networks, and those cases are silenced, they go unpunished,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights who represents Peña's family.
She said the case has exposed a criminal network “beyond what we can even imagine” and called for the state to provide answers on what happened to Peña.

item.title: Teachers strike in Paraguay to demand pension fund protections following bank's collapse
item.description:
Teachers strike in Paraguay to demand pension fund protections following bank's collapse
Thousands of public schoolteachers went on strike in Paraguay and took to the streets of several cities following the collapse of a major bank that resulted in the removal of the nation’s president last weekByThe Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 1:09 PM
Public schoolteachers went on strike in Paraguay Monday and took to the streets of several cities following the collapse of a major bank that resulted in the removal of the nation’s president last week.
Silvio Piris, the president of the Federation of Paraguayan Educators, said that teachers in Paraguay are concerned over the fate of around 60 million dollars in pensions funds that had been deposited in Ueno, the bank that was intervened by Paraguay’s government last week.
“We want the return of that money to be a priority,” Piris told Paraguay’s Channel 9.
More than 3 million people were frozen out of their bank accounts last Tuesday after Paraguay’s government intervened in Ueno Bank. Its closure has also affected pension funds and government-owned accounts.
The bank’s collapse led to the removal of Paraguayan President Santiago Peña, who was accused by legislators of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.
Peña was charged on Saturday with two crimes related to the bank's collapse, as an anti-corruption probe that also involves the former head of Paraguay’s central bank expands. The former president is being held at a military base while investigations continue. He has been replaced by his vice president, Pedro Alliana.

item.title: France blames Iran for the last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges
item.description:
France blames Iran for the last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges
France has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket fridges last monthByThe Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 12:11 PM
Share
PARIS -- France on Monday blamed Iran for last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges and summoned the Iranian ambassador, the French Foreign Ministry said.
In a statement, the ministry said: “France condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran against French interests.”
The Oct. 12 attack sent refrigerator temperatures soaring, affecting about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets.

item.title: How Mandela's ANC lost its way in South Africa and voters deserted it
item.description:
How Mandela's ANC lost its way in South Africa and voters deserted it
The African National Congress party in South Africa faces growing dissatisfaction and an exodus of supportersByGERALD IMRAY Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 10:54 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — The African National Congress once rose above politics in South Africa as a movement dedicated to freeing the country from the oppression of apartheid with the lofty principles of democracy, equality and a better life for all.
It was widely revered as a force for good when it became South Africa's ruling party in 1994 under Nelson Mandela, who was imprisoned for 27 years by the apartheid regime for his opposition to the system of racial segregation.
But three decades after the ANC transformed from a liberation movement to a political party in government, it faces growing dissatisfaction from South Africans who feel it has failed to live up to its promises.
Results released Sunday from last week’s local elections showed the party's share of the vote dropped 15 percentage points to just 31%, as South Africans rebuked it for failing to deliver basic services such as water and electricity.
The ANC, which once commanded 70% of the vote and had no challengers, conceded to being humbled in the local elections — its worst performance at the ballot box ever. The party's secretary-general called it a “catastrophic outcome” for the ANC and said it would enter a period of soul-searching to see how it could win back the trust of South Africa's people.
Two years ago, the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in a national election with 40% of the vote. It considered that a disaster, and a chance for self-reflection, but its supporters have continued to desert it.
While the end of apartheid gave every South African the right to vote and other basic freedoms, the challenge for the ANC was to convert that into a better standard of livi...

item.title: Ethnically split Cyprus' rival leaders agree to 2 more crossings across island's dividing line
item.description:
Ethnically split Cyprus' rival leaders agree to 2 more crossings across island's dividing line
The rival leaders of ethnically split Cyprus have agreed to open two new crossing points for vehicular traffic along a U.N.-controlled buffer zone in the first such development in nearly a decadeByMENELAOS HADJICOSTIS Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 10:34 AM
NICOSIA, Cyprus -- The rival leaders of the ethnically split island of Cyprus agreed on Monday to open two new crossing points for vehicular traffic along a U.N.-controlled buffer zone in the first such development in nearly a decade.
There are currently nine crossing points along the entire 180-kilometer (120-mile) length of the buffer zone that separates the breakaway Turkish Cypriot north from the Greek Cypriot south, where the internationally recognized government is seated.
Long lines of vehicles at some of these checkpoints have been a point of grievance for many, and it’s hoped that the two additional ones in the island’s northwest and southeast will help ease access for thousands who use them daily.
It’s not clear when the new crossing points will open but they will be launched simultaneously.
More notably, the agreement signifies tangible progress in talks between Greek Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman after months of discussions on trust-building measures that it's hoped will pave the way for a resumption of full-fledged negotiations to resolve the island’s ethnic divide.
Cyprus was split in 1974 when Turkey invaded after supporters of union with Greece mounted a coup backed by the Greek junta then ruling the country.
Turkish Cypriots declared independence in the island’s northern third in 1983, but only Turkey recognizes it and maintains more than 35,000 troops there.

item.title: Japan to provide coastal radar and drones to the Philippines under $27M deal
item.description:
Japan to provide coastal radar and drones to the Philippines under $27M deal
Japan said it will provide a coastal radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security aid deal, as both countries face growing tensions with ChinaByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 10:09 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan said it will provide a coastal surveillance radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security deal signed Monday, as the two defense partners face growing tensions with China.
Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Katsuro Kitagawa and Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro signed the 4.3 billion yen ($27 million) deal at a ceremony in Manila, Japan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The radar system will go to the Philippine Navy and the uncrewed aerial vehicles to the Philippine Air Force. The equipment is intended to strengthen maritime security and surveillance in the strategically important country, which sits near key sea lanes, the ministry said.
The deal marks the first transfer of finished Japanese-made defense equipment through Japan’s Official Security Assistance program. Established in 2023 as a military counterpart to its official development assistance program, OSA aims to help developing nations address challenges posed by China’s growing influence.
Japan has been accelerating its military and arms industry buildup. It lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports earlier this year and has agreed with the Philippines to begin talks on a deal that would allow Tokyo to provide used destroyers to Manila’s navy.
Separately on Monday, the leaders of Japan and Vietnam held talks in Tokyo and pledged to deepen cooperation in defense, energy and economic security amid China’s growing regional influence.

item.title: Russia's top independent newspaper closes after three decades, citing pressure
item.description:
Russia's top independent newspaper closes after three decades, citing pressure
Russia’s most celebrated independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, has closed its Moscow offices, citing relentless pressure from the governmentByThe Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 9:09 AM
Share
MOSCOW -- MOSCOW (AP) — Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials.
It was the last major independent media outlet critical of the Kremlin that remained active in Russia. Others closed or moved their operations abroad after President Vladimir Putin sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022.
In a statement published Oct. 30, the newspaper said the Russian authorities and the security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations.”
“Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime,” the newspaper said. "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot.”
Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta quickly became known for its fierce reporting and dedication to uncovering Russian human rights abuses and corruption. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War at the start of Putin’s first term as president. She was fatally shot in her apartment building in 2006.
On the newspaper's final day in its office Monday, journalists slowly removed the portraits of their slain colleagues from the newsroom where reporters and editors planned their work.
Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the outlet's closure almost every day for the past 4 1/2 years.
